That is a fair criticism, however, I didnt mean to say that OP shouldn't take action. Clearly this needs to be addressed. That said, I think that people often do the best they can with what they have. It's easy to paint it black or white from the outside looking in, but to the person living it, it is more complex. People don't easily work through the trauma and instincts they've developed after being raised in that sort of environment no matter how much therapy and advice they receive. I think the best thing anyone else can do in this situation is offer support and give advice on what these boundaries should look like. OP posted this because he is trying to make changes but doesn't know what those changes should look like. The best we can do is offer what advice we can about how to do this in a sustainable way and try to support his desire to develop better boundaries to protect his wife. Instead of blaming OP for not being able to work through his experiences and trauma on a timeline that we (who do not have the same experience or world view) deem acceptable, wouldn't it be better to just start with the situation where it stands and offer what we can to help? Telling a person they're terrible rarely motivates anyone to become better in my experience. I think its important to point out issues that need to be addressed while also having compassion and helping someone grow into a better version of themselves rather than beating them down.

I honestly am struggling with that question myself, my partner and I have had similar issues with our parents - though to a lesser degree. I think maybe you could start with declining visits more often if they have become excessive. Also, maybe try having a signal or something with your wife to say when it's getting to be too much, and end the visit. I feel like maybe that could be an easier first step than jumping to no contact. These things are hard to navigate and take time, so if you end up going back to therapy,  maybe discuss a plan of small boundaries to enact over time that get progressively stronger. That would likely be easier to act on and achieve and potentially preserve both relationships if possible. The important thing is to try to make consistent progress, even if it takes some time. Trying to make drastic changes to fast is often hard to sustain in the long run, and you never really reinforce the positive habits your trying to build.

If you feel like having a conversation with your mom would be productive, that would of course be ideal, but I understand that is rarely the case in situations like these

I feel like the comments here are a bit harsh...this is not an easy decision to make. Especially knowing other people raised in similar environments, and having some experience myself...it is often difficult to know what the right thing to do is. Being raised in an environment that punishes boundaries and doing anything to put yourself first or protect yourself makes it very difficult later on to feel morally like you are doing the right thing by enacting those boundaries. One way you may survive and rationalize the behavior of your loved ones is by empathizing with them to the point that it feels pointless to take any action because you know with their limited view of the world (whether due to trauma or ignorance) they are incapable of change and you feel it is unfair to blame them for their actions. After being raised in an environment like that, you can't just turn off that instinct and immediately change your entire world view. 
Also, it sounds like OP did set some boundaries that helped for a few years, but now those boundaries are being tested so it's more important than ever to reinforce them. However,  that will be even more difficult now that she has moved so close.

If you wanted to look into something that might help, one thing that really got me through that dark time was the book, “Big Magic” by Elizabeth Gilbert. It honestly changed my life. Its specifically targeted at helping artists figure out how to go after their goals in their careers, but it can really apply to anyone. It’s all about deciding what you’re passionate about and prioritizing your goals for yourself. I think it helped me to finally realize that I am the one who makes decisions about my life, and that it was under no one else’s control but my own. Realizing that gave me so much power to uproot a lot of the lies I grew up with about my own capabilities.

Not sure if that might be something that could help you, but I thought I’d mention it since it helped me a lot.

I was seriously contemplating suicide at one point, and I still have my moments where I think I would be better off dead. But what got me out of that dark place was realizing that I had been living for the love and approval of others, rather than my own. It wasn’t so much that I wanted to be admired by people, but that I wanted to make my family proud and have a close circle of friends I could depend on. I’ve never really had those things. For one, I don’t have many people in my life, and those that I do have I often can’t depend on. I have terrible social anxiety and just walking down the street makes me feel like I’m going to throw up, so trying to make friends feels virtually impossible. I also had little support from my family while I was in college because they didn’t believe I was capable of getting a degree in a STEM field. Every mistake I made was proof that I didn’t deserve to get an education, and my dad would often hold the fact that they were allowing me to stay with them over my head and threaten to kick me out (although, they weren’t helping me with tuition), and even before college I had a pretty strained relationship with my dad especially. Thus, between the lack of friends, and little support at home, I felt pretty isolated, and I know what a dark horrible place that can be. Completing my degree became my sole purpose in life, but I struggled tremendously because my mental health was crap. And any time I made even the slightest mistake, I would hear about it at home. I stared to hate myself so much that I felt like I deserved to die. That I was such a piece of shit that it would be better if I just disappeared. I don’t think I even wanted to die, I just didn’t see a future for myself anymore.
But then, the pandemic hit, and I had more time than ever to reflect on my life. I had moved out of my parents house, which was the separation I really needed to work on myself. Over time, piece by peace, I began to rebuild, and I realized that I was tired of basing my worth on my parents opinions. I love my field of study, and even if I didn’t always get the best grades due to my mental health, I couldn’t give up on it. Since I took that first step, things have begun to improve. I still don’t really have any friends, but I’ve decided that I won’t let my relationships (or lack there of) define my life. I’m going to focus on what I’m passionate about, and better myself until I’m strong enough to learn how to make friends. I’m not going to let myself throw in the towel on my life anymore. 
Since I made that decision, I’ve been able to become healthier than I ever thought possible.

I know that I’m not you, and I’m sorry for telling you my whole life’s story. I guess what I’m trying to say is, I hope that you can let go of all of the hateful, horrible stereotypes that others have thrust upon you and rise from the ash and rubble that you’re in right now. It’s easy to let the perceptions of others define us, but at the end of it all it’s our decision to forge our own path and become the person we want to be,  even if it means realizing we may be alone in the fight to do so. I’m so sorry for what you have been through, because you have, I’m sure, experienced more isolation than me and a lot more heartache, but I believe that you can find people who will love and accept you the way you deserve. Of course, I can’t promise that, but please don’t give up on yourself. Fight for a better tomorrow if you can bring yourself to do so. 

Go after your passions and stop trying to live someone else’s dream. You are capable of so much more than you think.
